title: SSH Keys — Concepts & Best Practices
text:
If you followed the SSH Setup page, you’ve already generated a key, copied it to ASC and Unity, and tested that ssh unity works without a password. This page is the deeper reference for everything keys: what they are, why they’re shaped the way they are, how to load them into your SSH agent, how to manage multiple keys, and how to recover when things go wrong.
You can read this top to bottom on your first time through, or treat it as a lookup when something breaks.

title: SSH Keys — Concepts & Best Practices
text:
When to use RSA instead
If you must interoperate with a very old system that doesn’t accept Ed25519:
ssh-keygen -t rsa -b 4096 -C "yourname@osu.edu" -f ~/.ssh/buckai_key_rsa
(-b 4096 means a 4096-bit RSA key — anything less is too short by modern standards.)
This is rare for OSU clusters in 2025. Stick with Ed25519 unless you hit a wall.

title: VS Code Remote-SSH + Claude Code on HPC
text:
This page walks through setting up a robust, persistent Claude Code workflow against OSU HPC clusters (ASC, Unity, OSC) through the ASC jumphost — using VS Code Remote-SSH as the editor and terminal host.
Audience: BuckAI students, postdocs, and collaborators who want to run Claude Code against files and compute resources living on a cluster reachable only through the ASC jumphost.
Prerequisites: A working SSH setup (see SSH Setup and SSH Keys) — you should already be able to ssh unity from a plain terminal with one Duo prompt and connection multiplexing in place.
crumbs: VS Code Remote-SSH + Claude Code on HPC

title: VS Code Remote-SSH + Claude Code on HPC
text:
6.1 Open the integrated terminal
Ctrl+` (control + backtick) opens the terminal panel. This terminal runs on the cluster, not on your Mac. You should see your usual cluster prompt.
crumbs: VS Code Remote-SSH + Claude Code on HPC

title: VS Code Remote-SSH + Claude Code on HPC
section: 6.2 Check that your config is loaded
text:
6.2 Check that your config is loaded
echo $ANTHROPIC_API_KEY    # should print your key
alias                       # should list your aliases
which claude                # should print path to Claude Code
If any of these are missing, your shell startup files aren’t being sourced correctly.
crumbs: VS Code Remote-SSH + Claude Code on HPC

title: VS Code Remote-SSH + Claude Code on HPC
text:
6.3 Common fix: source .bashrc from .bash_profile
Edit ~/.bash_profile on the cluster to ensure it sources .bashrc:
# At the end of ~/.bash_profile, add:
[ -f ~/.bashrc ] && source ~/.bashrc
The reason this matters: VS Code’s integrated terminal usually starts as a login shell on Linux, which reads ~/.bash_profile but not ~/.bashrc unless the former explicitly sources the latter.
crumbs: VS Code Remote-SSH + Claude Code on HPC

title: VS Code Remote-SSH + Claude Code on HPC
crumbs: VS Code Remote-SSH + Claude Code on HPC

title: VS Code Remote-SSH + Claude Code on HPC
text:
7.1 Auto-install (easiest)
The first time you run claude in VS Code’s integrated terminal while connected via Remote-SSH, the extension detects it and offers to install itself:
cd /path/to/your/project
claude
After a moment, VS Code prompts to install the Claude Code extension. Accept.
crumbs: VS Code Remote-SSH + Claude Code on HPC

title: VS Code Remote-SSH + Claude Code on HPC
text:
7.2 Manual install (if auto-install didn’t trigger)

Open the Extensions panel (Cmd+Shift+X)
Search for Claude Code
Install the official Anthropic extension
Critical: make sure it installs on the remote (cluster) side, not locally on your Mac. After installation, look at the Extensions panel — you’ll see two sections: Local - Installed and SSH: unity - Installed. Claude Code should appear under the SSH section. If it’s only local, click the extension and press Install in SSH: unity.
crumbs: VS Code Remote-SSH + Claude Code on HPC

title: VS Code Remote-SSH + Claude Code on HPC
text:
7.3 What the extension adds
Once installed, the following features become available:

Inline diff review: when Claude edits a file, VS Code’s native side-by-side diff viewer pops open. Accept or reject changes with a click instead of reading diffs in the terminal.
Selection-based prompting: highlight code in an editor pane, press Option+K (Mac), and an @file.py#L23-L45 reference is inserted into your Claude prompt.
Terminal output references: in your prompt, use @terminal:name to give Claude access to a terminal’s output without copy-pasting.
Problems panel access: Claude can see VS Code’s linter and compiler errors directly.
Dedicated chat panel: an alternative to the terminal interface, accessible via the Claude icon in the sidebar.
crumbs: VS Code Remote-SSH + Claude Code on HPC

title: VS Code Remote-SSH + Claude Code on HPC
text:
7.4 Optional: enable auto-save
Settings → search auto save → set Auto Save to afterDelay with delay 1000. This ensures that when Claude edits a file, your open editor reloads the changes without conflicting with unsaved buffer state.
crumbs: VS Code Remote-SSH + Claude Code on HPC

title: VS Code Remote-SSH + Claude Code on HPC
text:
8.1 The pattern
Each compute node gets its own Host block in ~/.ssh/config that uses Unity as a ProxyJump:
### Template for a compute node
Host u170
    HostName u170.asc.ohio-state.edu
    User yourname.##
    IdentityFile ~/.ssh/buckai_key
    IdentitiesOnly yes
    HostKeyAlgorithms +ssh-rsa
    PubkeyAcceptedAlgorithms +ssh-rsa
    ProxyJump unity
See SSH Setup §8 for the multi-hop multiplexing details.
crumbs: VS Code Remote-SSH + Claude Code on HPC

title: VS Code Remote-SSH + Claude Code on HPC
section: 8.2 Opening VS Code directly on a compute node
text:
8.2 Opening VS Code directly on a compute node
You can use VS Code Remote-SSH to connect to a compute node directly: in the Remote-SSH: Connect to Host dialog, type u170 (the alias) instead of unity. This gives you the full VS Code experience — editor, integrated terminal, Claude Code — running on the GPU node, with no port forwarding ceremony.
crumbs: VS Code Remote-SSH + Claude Code on HPC

title: VS Code Remote-SSH + Claude Code on HPC
text:
8.3 Port-forwarding shortcuts for Jupyter
If you’re running Jupyter on a compute node and want to view it in a browser on your laptop, a handy shell alias is:
alias jup170='ssh -L 9099:127.0.0.1:8888 u170'
This forwards your laptop’s port 9099 to the compute node’s port 8888 (where Jupyter listens). Open http://127.0.0.1:9099 in your browser to use the notebook.
crumbs: VS Code Remote-SSH + Claude Code on HPC

title: VS Code Remote-SSH + Claude Code on HPC
section: 8.4 When you don’t know the node in advance
text:
8.4 When you don’t know the node in advance
Slurm assigns interactive nodes dynamically, so for one-off sinteractive sessions you can’t pre-write a config block. In that case, do the allocation from a VS Code integrated terminal connected to Unity:
sinteractive -m 48000 -t 48:00:00 -g 1   # request a GPU node, say
Once allocated, you’re SSH’d to the compute node inside that terminal pane. For lighter-weight tools (Jupyter on the node, etc.), srun and port forwarding from inside the VS Code terminal is usually enough.
crumbs: VS Code Remote-SSH + Claude Code on HPC

title: VS Code Remote-SSH + Claude Code on HPC
text:
9.1 Starting a session

Open VS Code
Click the green corner in the bottom-left → Connect to Host → unity (or Cmd+Shift+P → Remote-SSH: Connect to Host)
Approve one Duo push
File → Open Recent → your project
Ctrl+` to open the integrated terminal
claude to start Claude Code

You’re now editing files on the cluster, with Claude Code running on the cluster, with diff review and selection prompting wired up.
crumbs: VS Code Remote-SSH + Claude Code on HPC

title: VS Code Remote-SSH + Claude Code on HPC
text:
9.2 The interaction model
You have two views of every file:

Editor pane (top): the file as you see it. Edit by hand, scroll, search, use language features.
Terminal pane (bottom) running claude: the conversational interface. Ask Claude to read, write, edit, run things.

When Claude edits a file:

The diff viewer appears
Review the proposed change
Accept (your file is updated on disk) or reject (file untouched)
If you have auto-save on and the file was already open in an editor pane, the editor reloads automatically

For longer code blocks, highlight the code in an editor pane and press Option+K — this inserts a precise @file#lines reference into your Claude prompt, avoiding copy-paste.
crumbs: VS Code Remote-SSH + Claude Code on HPC

title: VS Code Remote-SSH + Claude Code on HPC
text:
9.3 Running cluster jobs
Slurm commands work identically — they’re just running in a terminal on the cluster. From the integrated terminal:
sinteractive -m 48000 -t 48:00:00     # request an interactive node
squeue -u $USER                       # check your queue
sbatch myjob.slurm                    # submit a batch job
For long-running interactive work on a compute node, you can:

Open a second integrated terminal (click the + in the terminal panel), request an interactive node there, and run Claude Code on the compute node while the first terminal stays on the login node for monitoring
Or wrap sinteractive in tmux so the allocation survives disconnects
crumbs: VS Code Remote-SSH + Claude Code on HPC

title: VS Code Remote-SSH + Claude Code on HPC
text:
9.4 Pausing work
You can safely:

✔ Close your laptop lid — VS Code’s remote server keeps running on the cluster. Reopen, the connection re-establishes automatically, terminals are still there with full state.
✔ Disconnect from WiFi — same as above. VS Code reconnects when the network returns.
⚠ Quit VS Code entirely — your terminals on the cluster die, so Claude Code’s session ends. To survive a full quit, run claude inside tmux on the cluster (which works fine inside VS Code’s terminal too).
crumbs: VS Code Remote-SSH + Claude Code on HPC

title: VS Code Remote-SSH + Claude Code on HPC
text:
9.5 Ending a session

Save any open files (Cmd+S, or with auto-save it’s already done)
In the Claude Code terminal, type /exit to cleanly end the session
File → Close Window — VS Code keeps the remote server running for ~10 minutes in case you reconnect, then shuts it down

To force immediate disconnect: Cmd+Shift+P → Remote-SSH: Kill VS Code Server on Host.
crumbs: VS Code Remote-SSH + Claude Code on HPC

title: SSH Setup for ASC and Unity (Complete Beginner-Friendly Guide)
text:
High-performance computing (HPC) clusters like ASC and Unity at OSU are accessed using a tool called SSH (Secure Shell). SSH lets you log in to remote computers securely and run commands as if you were sitting at that machine.
Because OSU clusters are protected behind institutional firewalls, you cannot log in directly. Instead, you must:

connect first to a jump host (a secure gateway machine), then
from there connect to Unity or compute nodes like u126, u170, u181, etc.

SSH can automatically perform these multi-step hops for you — and skip extra Duo prompts along the way — but only if your setup is correct.
This guide walks through everything you need:
✔ Understanding SSH keys at a high level (see SSH Keys for the deep dive) ✔ Why clusters use jump hosts ✔ How to generate a secure key pair ✔ How to upload your key to OSU systems ✔ How to configure SSH so you can just type:
ssh unity
✔ How to set up connection multiplexing so Duo prompts you only once ✔ Troubleshooting and common mistakes
It is designed for students and postdocs with zero prior HPC experience.
crumbs: SSH Setup for ASC and Unity (Complete Beginner-Friendly Guide)

title: SSH Setup for ASC and Unity (Complete Beginner-Friendly Guide)
text:
4.1 Install on ASC Jump Host
ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/buckai_key.pub yourname.##@jump.asc.ohio-state.edu -p 2200
You will enter your OSU password once here.
crumbs: SSH Setup for ASC and Unity (Complete Beginner-Friendly Guide)

title: SSH Setup for ASC and Unity (Complete Beginner-Friendly Guide)
text:
4.2 Install on Unity Login Node
ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/buckai_key.pub yourname.##@unity.asc.ohio-state.edu
After these two steps, your key is recognized on OSU systems.
crumbs: SSH Setup for ASC and Unity (Complete Beginner-Friendly Guide)

title: SSH Setup for ASC and Unity (Complete Beginner-Friendly Guide)
section: 5.1 Prepare ~/.ssh/ and create a sockets directory
text:
5.1 Prepare ~/.ssh/ and create a sockets directory
The sockets directory is where SSH will store small files used to share one authenticated connection across many sessions. Without it, you can’t get the “one Duo tap, everything else is free” experience.
mkdir -p ~/.ssh
chmod 700 ~/.ssh
mkdir -p ~/.ssh/sockets
chmod 700 ~/.ssh/sockets
touch ~/.ssh/config
chmod 600 ~/.ssh/config
Permissions matter — SSH silently ignores the config file if it is world-readable.
crumbs: SSH Setup for ASC and Unity (Complete Beginner-Friendly Guide)

title: SSH Setup for ASC and Unity (Complete Beginner-Friendly Guide)
text:
5.2 Open the config
nano ~/.ssh/config
crumbs: SSH Setup for ASC and Unity (Complete Beginner-Friendly Guide)

title: SSH Setup for ASC and Unity (Complete Beginner-Friendly Guide)
text:
5.3 Add the full template
Paste the following (replace yourname.## with your OSU username, e.g. smith.123):
### Global defaults: apply to ALL hosts
Host *
    # Connection multiplexing: authenticate once, reuse the connection
    ControlMaster auto
    ControlPath ~/.ssh/sockets/%r@%h:%p
    ControlPersist 10m

    # Keepalives: prevent firewalls/NAT from dropping idle connections
    ServerAliveInterval 30
    ServerAliveCountMax 4
    TCPKeepAlive yes

    # Prefer your SSH agent + macOS Keychain (so keys stay loaded across sessions)
    AddKeysToAgent yes
    UseKeychain yes

### ASC Jumphost (requires Duo MFA)
Host ascjumphost
    HostName jump.asc.ohio-state.edu
    User yourname.##
    Port 2200
    IdentityFile ~/.ssh/buckai_key
    IdentitiesOnly yes

### Unity Login Node (via jump host)
Host unity
    HostName unity.asc.ohio-state.edu
    User yourname.##
    IdentityFile ~/.ssh/buckai_key
    IdentitiesOnly yes
    ProxyJump ascjumphost
    # Older HPC SSH daemons may need these for key-based auth to work:
    HostKeyAlgorithms +ssh-rsa
    PubkeyAcceptedAlgorithms +ssh-rsa
Now typing:
ssh unity
automatically performs:
Laptop → Jump Host → Unity
with one Duo prompt and zero password typing.
crumbs: SSH Setup for ASC and Unity (Complete Beginner-Friendly Guide)

title: SSH Setup for ASC and Unity (Complete Beginner-Friendly Guide)
text:
6.1 Connection multiplexing (the Duo painkiller)
ControlMaster auto
ControlPath ~/.ssh/sockets/%r@%h:%p
ControlPersist 10m
Together these tell SSH:

The first SSH connection to a host authenticates normally (Duo and all) and creates a Unix socket at ~/.ssh/sockets/...
Any subsequent SSH connections to the same host reuse that socket and skip authentication entirely
The master connection stays alive for 10 minutes after the last session closes, so quick reconnects don’t re-prompt for Duo

This is critical for VS Code Remote-SSH, which opens multiple parallel connections during connect — without multiplexing, each one triggers a separate Duo prompt and they race each other to timeout.
crumbs: SSH Setup for ASC and Unity (Complete Beginner-Friendly Guide)

title: SSH Setup for ASC and Unity (Complete Beginner-Friendly Guide)
text:
6.2 Keepalives — the counterintuitive part
ServerAliveInterval 30
ServerAliveCountMax 4
The intuition “bigger numbers = stays alive longer” is backwards.

ServerAliveInterval 30 means: every 30 seconds of idleness, the SSH client sends a small “are you there?” probe.
ServerAliveCountMax 4 means: if 4 consecutive probes get no response, give up and disconnect.

So this tolerates up to 2 minutes (4 × 30s) of server silence. The probes themselves are what keep the connection alive — they prevent firewalls and NAT devices from forgetting your connection during idle periods.
A larger ServerAliveInterval is less protective, not more, because middleboxes have more time to forget you between probes.
If you want maximum durability, keep ServerAliveInterval small (15–30s) and crank ServerAliveCountMax up (e.g. to 120) to tolerate long server silences.
crumbs: SSH Setup for ASC and Unity (Complete Beginner-Friendly Guide)

title: SSH Setup for ASC and Unity (Complete Beginner-Friendly Guide)
text:
6.3 Why the +ssh-rsa lines?
Modern OpenSSH (9.0+) disabled the ssh-rsa signature algorithm by default for security reasons, but many HPC clusters still use server keys that rely on it. Without these lines you may see errors like:
no matching host key type found. Their offer: ssh-rsa
The + prefix means “add to the default list” rather than “replace it,” so modern algorithms still take priority — ssh-rsa is just available as a fallback. Keep these lines on cluster connections until your sysadmin confirms server keys have been rotated.
crumbs: SSH Setup for ASC and Unity (Complete Beginner-Friendly Guide)

title: SSH Setup for ASC and Unity (Complete Beginner-Friendly Guide)
text:
Multi-hop multiplexing in practice
With three levels of hops (laptop → ascjumphost → unity → u170), the multiplexing in the global Host * block helps each hop independently:

First time: Duo prompt at ascjumphost, key auth at unity, key auth at u170
Subsequent ssh u170, ssh u139, etc. within 10 minutes: zero prompts — the ascjumphost socket is reused, the unity socket is reused, only the final hop’s key auth happens

This is what makes a half-dozen named compute-node aliases practical.
crumbs: SSH Setup for ASC and Unity (Complete Beginner-Friendly Guide)
